newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. accused of complicity in Colombia's "dirty war".
newsitem.headline: U.S. accused of complicity in Colombia's "dirty war".

text.p: A leading human rights group called on Sunday for an immediate end to U.S. military aid to Colombia in a scathing report accusing Washington of official complicity in the country's "dirty war" against suspected leftist rebel sympathisers.

The report by New York-based Human Rights Watch, entitled "Colombia's Killer Networks," echoed similar charges about an unholy alliance between Colombia's military and right-wing paramilitary groups -- or death squads -- made last month by Amnesty International.

Senior Colombia and military officials have long insisted that no such alliance existed. But human rights groups said there was overwhelming evidence to the contrary and that the United States was a wilful partner in its coverup.

"It's time to clear the smoke screen of official denial and identify the military-paramilitary partnership for what it is," Jose Miguel Vivanco, executive director of Human Rights Watch/ Americas, said in a statement.

"This is a sophisticated mechanism, in part supported by years of advice, training, weaponry and official silence by the United States, that allows the Colombian military to fight a dirty war and Colombian officialdom to deny it," he said.
"The price so far is thousands of dead, disappeared, maimed and terrorised Colombians," he added.

In its report Human Rights Watch alleges that a team put together by the CIA and U.S. Defence Department worked with the Colombian military on the restructuring of its intelligence- gathering capabilities in 1991 in an effort that led directly to the creation of paramilitary "killer networks."

Additionally it said Washington provided weapons, ostensibly to fight drugs, to Colombian military units with a record of serious human rights abuse without establishing mechanisms to ensure that U.S. aid was not used to commit further rights abuse.

"The evidence cited in this report, including confidential Colombian and declassified U.S. government documents, raises serious questions about the United States's contribution to the military-paramilitary partnership in Colombia," Joost Hiltermann, executive director of the Human Rights Watch Arms Project, which co-authored the report, said in a statement.
"Under the stated objective of fighting drugs, the United States has lent Colombia's military and their paramilitary partners significant support," he said.

"Although credible reports of human rights abuses are common, the U.S. appears to have turned a blind eye to them, ignoring the fact that U.S. weapons, advice, and training have gone to forces that routinely commit human rights violations, often in partnership with paramilitaries."

The report urged the immediate suspension of all U.S. military aid, arms sales and military training to Colombia -- a country immersed in a low-intensity war with leftist guerrillas since the mid-1960s -- and said such aid should not be resumed "until the longstanding practices of gross and persistent violations of human rights by the Colombian armed forces and their paramilitary partners have ceased."

It also urged an immediate and comprehensive investigation of U.S. security assistance to Colombia since 1990 "to determine the extent to which the United States has become complicit in Colombia's killer networks."
